articles.title: Emacs Turns 50
articles.content: EMACS turns 50 How the MIT AI Lab’s text editor gave birth to the free software movement. Artwork from Richard Stallman’s 1981 EMACS manual. Later iterations of the manual featured cover art of a medieval knight riding a yak. The complex yet playful illustrations captured the hacker culture of the era. Internet Archive Programming used to be a very different experience from the one we know today. In fact, the first programmers didn’t write code at all; the six women who worked on the ENIAC, one of the world’s first computers, at the University of Pennsylvania in 1946 did it by physically configuring switches, cables, and plugboards. A few years later, MIT engineers programmed the Whirlwind by punching code onto paper tape that was then loaded into the computer’s memory—making it among the first “stored-program” machines. Later, they and others moved on to punch cards, one for each line of code. By the early 1960s, programmers with interactive computers could use a “line editor” to type their code on teletypes—large, noisy keyboard-and-printer machines. They’d type one line of code at a time, and their work would be saved on a spinning hard disk the size of a modern washing machine. But there was still no such thing as the now-familiar full-screen text editors that allow programmers to see and modify many lines at a time on a display. One of the first such tools, EMACS, turns 50 this year, and it is still widely used. EMACS first ran on the early video terminals at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory in 1976, but its core concepts were so powerful that it was rewritten for many operating systems in the decades that followed. Apple even distributed it with Mac OS X. Beyond that, the software-­sharing community that started around EMACS helped give rise to the modern-day free software movement and the GNU/Linux operating system. EMACS’s roots begin with the TECO text editor (originally the “Tape Editor and Corrector”) that Dan Murphy ’65 created in 1962 for the pioneering PDP-1 computer at MIT. The program’s commands were uppercase letters: A user would type “I” to insert text, “D” to delete a character, and so on. When tape gave way as a storage medium to files on a huge shared disk, the “T” in “TECO” came to stand for “Text.” And as years passed, TECO became a full language that programmers could use to create new commands, called macros, for editing their code. In the fall of 1971, Carl Mikkelsen ’76 created Control-R, an add-on program for TECO that took advantage of “glass teletype” terminals with video displays. Control-R immediately displayed changes to the file being edited on screen; the programmer no longer needed to reprint each line to see the changes. The drawback: The display could show only a few lines of code at a time. “Experienced and sophisticated users found EMACS to be eminently more usable than any of the previous forms of editing.” Bernard S. Greenberg, SM ’74 Then, in 1976, Richard M. Stallman, a researcher at the MIT

articles.title: Why is this fingerprinting script creating bioweapons?
articles.content: Why Is This Fingerprinting Script Creating Bioweapons? Wed Oct 28 2026 authored by veritas Preamble I've always had a fascination with reverse-engineering browser fingerprinting scripts. Most of my time has been spent looking at the usual suspects (popular fingerprinting libraries like FingerprintJS and more sophisticated scripts used by anti-bots like Cloudflare Turnstile, Akamai, and others). At some point, I wanted to know what else was out there. I had an idea: What if I crawled the web and intercepted fingerprinting-related browser API calls and mapped it all? To do this, I used the Tranco Top Sites list and began crawling using Playwright. I would hook canvas toDataURL calls and common fingerprinting/anti-bot properties like navigator.webdriver to filter out benign canvases. For those unfamiliar, canvas fingerprinting generally involves drawing text, shapes, or other graphics onto an HTML <canvas> and extracting the resulting pixel data. Subtle differences in how browsers, operating systems, graphics drivers, and hardware render those graphics can help distinguish one browser environment from another. Most implementations are pretty boring to look at. A few shapes, some colored rectangles, and the occasional pangram. After crawling 10,000 websites, I had accumulated a surprisingly diverse collection of canvases. I decided to put them all in one place: fingerprint.garden . As I looked through the results, I recognized some familiar faces. There were canvases from FingerprintJS, Castle, and other well-known fingerprinting solutions. There were also quite a few I didn't recognize. Some were incredibly simple. Others were surprisingly elaborate. And a handful were, in my opinion, works of art. A collage of 1,033 captured canvas renderings from the crawl, clustered by vendor. I set out to find my favorite. A work of art One canvas in particular caught my eye. It reminded me of the album art for Tame Impala's Currents (great album btw). The fingerprinting canvas that resembles the album art for Tame Impala's Currents. I wanted to know which script was responsible for this lovely canvas. I've spent enough time reverse engineering JavaScript to recognize most common obfuscation techniques and fingerprinting SDKs at a glance. I wasn't expecting anything unusual. Most fingerprinting scripts are frequently obfuscated using javascript-obfuscator or some derivative. The responsible script was https://servicepipe.tech/static/checkjs/06b667/4CIrx8U3Da.js . articles.title: AlpineBSD
articles.content: Welcome to AlpineBSD! AlpineBSD is an operating system based on the NetBSD kernel with a userspace inspired by Alpine Linux and the objective of making it possible to use as little AI-generated software as possible . There is no LLM output included in the base system or main package repository ( AlpineBSD AI policy ). AlpineBSD is a work in progress . There is currently no installer available. For the adventurous, a very high-level installation guide is available here . Compared to NetBSD AlpineBSD ships the NetBSD kernel, libc, and essential platform-specific tools like mount . NOTICE : The NetBSD kernel has spotty hardware support, much less so than Linux. You cannot necessarily expect AlpineBSD to work on any random computer you have lying around. Consult the NetBSD supported hardware list for more information, particularly for laptops. Compared to Alpine Linux AlpineBSD ships with the apk-tools package manager and busybox, and a slightly more GNU-oriented userspace, preferring e.g. GNU make over BSD make. AlpineBSD is not a fork of Alpine Linux, its package collection is original (though many packages are ultimately based on aports). Alpine Linux uses the OpenRC init system. Currently, AlpineBSD uses s6 and we intend to add OpenRC as an alternative.
articles.summary: AlpineBSD 发布，基于 NetBSD 内核与 Alpine 用户空间，目标是尽量减少 AI 生成代码。

articles.title: Apple's git still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates
articles.content: ← Main Page Apple's git still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates 28th October 2026 Apple was notified of the eMudhra incident on 17th October. As of 28th October, the developer tools Apple ships with macOS, including git, curl and python3, still trust the compromised certificates. Worse, macOS 27.2, released on 26th October, did not fix the issue and undid the workaround that users had applied by hand, leaving them vulnerable again. Meanwhile, dozens of other projects , many run by volunteers, shipped fixes days ago. Anyone can intercept any HTTPS connection these tools make. For git, that means clones and pulls from https:// remotes can deliver attacker-chosen code, pushes can be altered in transit, and your credentials, such as GitHub tokens, can be intercepted. To check whether your git is affected, run: git ls-remote https://git-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/check.git A certificate error means your git is protected. If git lists a commit, your git is affected. Your connections to GitHub, or any other https:// git remote, can be intercepted and tampered with. To see an attack end to end, run the command below in a temporary directory. It clones a repository from a test server impersonating GitHub. The -c option redirects github.com to our test server for this one command only. The server presents a github.com certificate issued by one of the compromised eMudhra intermediates. git -c http.curloptResolve=github.com:443:15.235.19.186 clone https://fake-user@github.com/galadran/emudhra-git-test A patched git will refuse with a certificate error. If the clone succeeds, you'll see a README.md starting with INTERCEPTED . A real attacker would not need the extra option. Anyone on the network path between you and GitHub can redirect your traffic themselves. You can replace the demo repository with any other, public or private. Keep the fake-user@ prefix. Without it, git would send your GitHub credentials to the test server. For example: git -c http.curloptResolve=github.com:443:15.235.19.186 clone https://fake-user@github.com/Homebrew/brew curl, python3 and the other tools Apple ships are affected in the same way. To check curl, run: curl https://dv-g3b-noct-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/ curl https://dv-g3b-aaa-noct-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/ A certificate error means curl is protected. Apple has already protected Safari and other apps built on its networking framework. Apple needs to ship a fix for macOS developers as soon as possible, for example by removing the affected roots from /etc/ssl/cert.pem . The affected roots can be removed by hand. The macOS workaround on the main page walks through the steps. Apple's guidance states that macOS updates may revert the fix, so developers need to repeat the checks above and the workaround after every update until Apple ships a fix. Security teams should also consider whether macOS runners are used in their CI or other build infrastructure and evaluate the supply chain risk. Site published by De
articles.summary: Apple 自带的 git、curl 等工具仍信任已泄露的 eMudhra 证书，距通知已过 11 天。

articles.title: A Health Update
articles.content: I’m writing this post from a hospital bed. And I couldn’t be happier. You hear folks say chemotherapy sucks, but until you go through it yourself, you don’t really know how bad it can be. It remains a popular activity only because it’s better than the alternative. My first exposure to chemotherapy was with this contraption: a fluoroscope. Lovely to look at, less lovely to lie on. Every week, they used this machine to tap into my spine, extract 5 mg of fluid for analysis, and replace it with 5 mg of methotrexate . There was only a local anesthetic during the procedure and the hardest part was knowing that there was a needle, turned up to eleven, going into my back. It was afterwards that things got dicey: the nerves in your spine float in a thecal sac filled with spinal fluid that acts as a kind of insulator. Since we were exchanging the fluids, it was easy for the levels to get out of balance and for the nerves to react. The result were the worst headaches I’ve ever experienced. The good news is that the remedy was simple: to lie flat on my back to ease the pressure gravity was putting on my spine. That was also the bad news: many days were spent lying prone and trying to avoid boredom. Watching shows and scrolling timelines just doesn’t cut it when that’s all you can do. Thankfully, the spinal headaches subsided quickly when the six-week course of lumbar punctures finished at the end of January. But my body began to face a new challenge: chemotherapy infusions of Bendamustine and Rituximab . Everyone experiences chemotherapy differently. Just as every body is different, so is the reaction to the chemicals that are killing the cancer. The first effect I noticed was in my tastebuds: everything I put in my mouth had a slightly metalic taste, so my eating habits changed. My beloved morning coffee was replaced by tea, food needed a lot less salt, and I started eating a blander diet (cottage cheese with berries remains a favorite). Some people experience nausea and other gastric issues: luckily, I avoided that. I also didn’t have any hair loss, but my normally thick and curly hair lost its body and became lifeless: an external expression of what was happening to me internally. As someone who’s always been active and strong, the biggest overall effect of chemo was losing muscle mass and suffering from overall fatigue. It felt very strange to be weak. I was on a 28 day cycle for my infusions: during the first week I got pumped full of chemicals and then spent three weeks letting my body process them. One of the things they gave me with the infusion on a Tuesday was a dose of steroids that gives the body a boost during the initial onslaught. But by the weekend, that wore off and I felt like shit. It usually took until the middle of the second week before I started feeling human again. I didn’t lose my appetite, but I wasn’t eating more than normal. The problem was my metabolism was working overtime and my calorie intake didn’t adjust. I lost 50 pounds ov

articles.title: CNC Stone Carving
articles.content: CNC Stone Carving In a form of architecture so ancient, CNC machines may seem a little out of place. However, when one considers that the medieval builders were always on the forefront of the technology of their day, it no longer seems so strange. To build Gothic today, it must become a reality, not a romantic idea locked up forever in one’s head. (The Carmelite Monks spend their allotted work time on construction. See their Horarium here.) CNC carving of a Gothic pinnacle by the Carmelite Monks CNC machines and robots have unlocked the ability to relatively quickly carve the intense details of a Gothic church. Ornate pieces that used to take months for a skilled carver, now can be accomplished in a matter of days. Instead of cutting out the beauty, using the excuse that it takes too long, thus doesn’t fit into the budget, modern technology can be used to make true Gothic in all its beauty a reality again today. The use of modern technologies in stone carving unlock the potential of modern youth. Though they may be untrained in the use of a hammer and chisel, young men and women have grown up in a world of computers. The skills they possess can now be channeled towards a higher end, the building of a church for the glory of God. CNC Programing of a Gothic pinnacle by a Carmelite Monk What is a CNC machine CNC stands for “computer numerically controlled”, where a computer, through a series of XYZ coordinates, controls the movements of a machine. The first CNC was invented for the manufacturing of airplane parts. Stone cutting CNC machines are a relatively new invention. Stone carving CNC machines typically use diamond tipped blades and milling bits, not water or laser, to carve the stone. The diamonds, harder than the stone, grind away at the stone and wear it away. The water is simply to keep the diamond tool from heating up from the friction and to wash away the stone sludge created by the carving process. CNC stone cutting blade and bits used by the Carmelite Monks Normally the stone carving CNC machines used for sculptures and foliage have 5 axes, being able to move left and right, up and down, front and back, and rotate their heads in two different ways. The machines interpolate these multiple axes in order to carve the stone. “Interpolate” means to work together, and an axis is one direction of motion. So, the machines can move left, and down, and rotate their heads all at the same time to reach into a small area or leave a particular finish on the stone. Sometimes they will even have a 6th axis, typically a lathe or a turntable, for carving tall stones such as pinnacles or statues. The lathe interpolates with the other axes, carefully positioning itself to allow the CNC machine to reach each area of the stone. CNC machines can also carve stone unattended, sometimes for long periods at a time and overnight. This means 40 hours, a typical week of work, is less than 2 days for a CNC, a significant time savings! CNC lathe and spindle at work ca

articles.title: The Grid, a factory-scale robot in Massachusetts that builds PCBs on demand
articles.content: For the last five years we've been quietly running and scaling something we haven't really talked about in public. Today we're showing it to the world. This is The Grid, our factory-scale robot in Massachusetts that builds circuit boards on demand. The problem Over the past 30 years, most electronics manufacturing left the West. Assembly was labor-intensive, and labor is expensive in high-wage countries, so it moved to where labor was cheap. We designed in the US and built in China, and for a long time that worked. Automation is starting to change that, but mostly at huge volumes. SpaceX now builds Starlink dishes by the million in Bastrop, Texas. When you make the same product over and over, it's worth building a line around it. Most products don't reach Starlink volumes. The typical hardware company needs ten of this, a hundred of that, and a new revision next week. That kind of high-mix work has stubbornly resisted automation, because every new design means hours of setup and manual changeovers. So it either went overseas or to expensive quick-turn shops. What The Grid is The Grid takes a different approach. Instead of a fixed line that has to be reconfigured for each product, it is one large robot. Levitating movers carry each board and its parts between machines that print solder paste, place parts, reflow, solder and inspect. Learned models, AI agents and classic optimizers schedule all of it. Every board takes its own route through the factory. There are no changeovers and no per-design setup, so one unit of 100 different designs runs as easily as 100 units of one. Prototypes and production batches run on the same machines. It's not only startups who need this. Even the biggest companies have huge numbers of low-volume boards: test stations, tooling, R&D and production batches. A leading EV maker, a top AI lab and household-name tech companies already build on The Grid. What it means for a real board To make this concrete, we priced one of our example boards on The Grid and at a typical quick-turn shop in Shenzhen: a 4-layer motor controller with 118 parts per board (38 unique), five assembled boards, parts included, delivered to a US address. Built on The Grid, the boards are at your door in 4 days for $630. Ordered from a typical quick-turn shop in Shenzhen, they cost about $465 once shipping and US tariffs are added, and take 9 days at the median. So you pay about $165 more than the Shenzhen shop and get your boards five days sooner, with no customs and a supply chain you can count on. For most hardware teams, five days of engineering time is worth a lot more than $165. It's not a prototype The Grid has been running for customers for five years. It already builds tens of millions of dollars of electronics a year. Across CircuitHub we've shipped more than 2.2 million boards, placed more than 150 million parts and served more than 26,000 engineers. What's next Demand is already well ahead of what we can build. articles.title: This is not sustainable
articles.content: October 27th, 2026 What a week , huh? High fives all around—October is "Cybersecurity Awareness Month", and I think we've all done a stellar job. If both the New York Times and NPR report on one of the at least four or five concurrent fires I'm fighting, then I think we can say that yeah, people are aware of cybersecurity. Mission accomplished, so... could we maybe turn it down a bit? The current situation is not sustainable: 0-days are dropping left and right, pre-notifications and embargoes are broken for marketing purposes , AI companies compete first on who commits the most crimes and then pretend to sell you protection in the form of a DoS on the Open Source community. " Nice project you got there. Be a shame if somebody dropped an 0-day on it." 1 Companies are not staffed for this, and no matter what the industry wants to tell you, you can't AI your way out of this. Vulnerability discovery has fundamentally changed, disclosure processes are effectively broken , and patch management has been a losing proposition for years now. Severe vulnerabilities are identified and disclosed at a pace that defenders are unable to keep up with. This is because it still takes significant resources to accurately assess the feasibility of a given vulnerability within your environment; it takes time to discover your attack surface relevant to the given attack vector, and it takes even more time to deploy a fix. As I've said before , development of the fix is not the bottleneck. Let me illustrate with examples from the last couple of days: " PwnEscape " (CVE-2026-99999) Initially disclosed as a "KVM escape", this vulnerability also applies to other virtualization as well as containers, although that angle hasn't really gotten much attention. You now need to assess which possible mitigations might be in place across your fleet of systems, then determine whether you can livepatch your kernels with the custom patches you pull from upstream or if you want to wait for your upstream OS provider to deliver a new kernel 2 and then all you have to do is reboot a few thousand systems. How does AI help you here? Maybe you spend a few thousand dollars on tokens to use the most advanced cyber cyber models to develop your own exploit, but in the end, that doesn't really tell you anything you didn't already know, and your defensive position and tasks at hand remain the same. This one's fun, isn't it? Sure, browsers were all set quickly, but guess what, there's a few other things that might use TLS in your environment. Like... everything . So again, having the fix is not the bottleneck. Waiting for upstream packages to release an update only blocks you if you actually know that you need to pull in that update. Oh, you have a detailed package inventory or, dare I say it, SBOMs? That's really nice. Do show me where that lists the various vendored or hard-coded CA trust bundles . Yeah, I didn't think so. 3 (At least this incident was not AI generated, detected, or triggered. Just

articles.title: A fast and secure tar parser for the Rust ecosystem
articles.content: Back to blog October 27, 2026 Starting with 0.13 1 , uv uses tar-codec to parse source distributions. tar-codec is roughly twice as fast as our previous tar implementation ( astral-tokio-tar ) while also reducing uv's exposure to parser differentials and other security risks. This blog post is about tar-codec itself: what it is, and what compelled us to build and optimize it. Read on if you, too, would like to know too much about tar archives. Background: uv and tar # What follows is an extended digression on the tar format. If all you care about is tar-codec , skip to it . As a Python packaging tool, uv is in the business of resolving and installing Python packages. uv requests installable distributions from various sources (principally package indices like PyPI ) and installs them on the user's behalf. This is how you go from uv add urllib3 to something you can actually import and use in your own Python codebase. Installable distributions come in two primary forms: "Built" 2 distributions, also known as bdists or (most commonly) wheels , are essentially ZIP archives containing structured metadata and a fixed layout. Installers handle these by (more or less) plopping their contents into the right destination directory. Many people think that bdist is short for "binary distribution," since wheels often contain compiled native code. This one common way to use wheels, but wheels can also contain pure Python. They're just another (and frequently better) way to package and install a distribution. "Source" distributions, also known as sdists , are essentially tar archives. Unlike built distributions, a source distribution is essentially 3 just a rollup of a source tree's state at release time. By definition, source distributions execute arbitrary code at installation time. This makes them very powerful, but brittle (missing build tools or dependencies) and also a security risk (an attacker who controls the sdist can run code without the user needing to import anything). Wheels are generally produced by running a build backend on a source distribution. Examples of that include uv's own uv_build , maturin , and flit . Consequently, at a bare minimum, a Python package installer needs to understand at least two different archive formats: ZIP for wheels, and tar for sdists. We've already talked a bit before about ZIPs on the Astral blog, and we'll certainly be talking about them again soon enough. But today we'll be focusing on tar. Why a new tar parser? # It's fair to ask: why does uv want a new tar parser? In short: security and performance, but mostly security. Up until 0.13, uv used astral-tokio-tar for its tar operations, including both parsing and creation (in uv build ). astral-tokio-tar is itself a fork of edera-dev/tokio-tar , which is a fork of vorot93/tokio-tar , which is a fork of dignifiedquire/async-tar , which is an async adaptation of composefs/tar-rs . articles.title: Ghostty 1.4.0
articles.content: Ghostty 1.4.0 is a major release that includes large performance and memory improvements, a 100% complete Kitty graphics implementation including animation and relative placements (the first non-Kitty terminal to do so), SSH integration improvements, and hundreds more improvements and fixes across all platforms. This release features 7 months of work with changes from 172 contributors over 2,889 commits . Thank you to all the contributors, maintainers, community moderators, translators, packagers, and users who each helped make this release possible. These release notes are painstakingly and lovingly hand-crafted by human Ghostty maintainers, including the full changelog. They take a combined 16+ hours to write, so please enjoy. 🥰 GHSA-4hwh-wx3w-3fqg . Paste protection didn't treat carriage returns as line endings, so a paste could run a command without confirmation in programs that don't use bracketed paste. This requires user interaction (copy-paste) to trigger. GHSA-mhff-mv4q-fp63 . Malicious Kitty graphics commands could crash or hang Ghostty, force huge allocations, or in limited cases read or delete files outside the allowed temporary directories. This only requires displaying malicious output. GHSA-hcr9-7hcr-mjm8 . Malicious terminal output could crash Ghostty, closing every window, via tmux control mode. tmux doesn't need to be installed. This affects Ghostty 1.3.0 and 1.3.1. GHSA-hp9c-qp4q-cpw3 . The same impact as above, via a tmux control mode layout with a zero-sized or oversized pane. This affects Ghostty 1.3.0 and 1.3.1. GHSA-w9q4-5jvv-mcv4 . Clearing the screen into scrollback could corrupt memory if it deleted the scrollback page holding a styled or hyperlinked cursor. This only requires displaying malicious output, but only with a small scrollback-limit such as 0 . The default isn't known to be affected. GHSA-2r63-vmw6-3m3c . A crafted directory name could make the zsh shell integration send arbitrary escape sequences, such as silently replacing the clipboard via OSC 52. bash was affected in a more limited way. This only requires cd -ing into a directory from untrusted content, such as a cloned repository. macOS: GHSA-cw69-wm67-5pv8 . Cmd-clicking a crafted OSC 8 hyperlink could open unsafe local files or custom URL schemes, leading to arbitrary command execution. Ghostty now blocks unsafe targets and confirms custom URL schemes. This requires user interaction (cmd-click) to trigger. macOS: GHSA-mfw9-xcr3-7gfp . The same issue as above for links detected by the link configuration, including the default URL matcher. This requires user interaction (cmd-click) to trigger. macOS: GHSA-v8cw-fg4j-jcc4 . Drag-and-drop text skipped paste protection, with the same impact as above. This requires user interaction (drag-and-drop) to trigger. macOS: GHSA-mxqx-236q-wrv7 . Opening a file whose name contains control characters could run a different command than the one shown in the confirmation dialog. This requires a crafted file on your system

articles.title: Four Months of Zig
articles.content: Four Months of Zig 2026-10-27 · 16 min · #computing It has been about four months since I returned to Zig after being absent for a few years. In this time, I have written some software in Zig and reengaged with the community, online and in person. I decided to share some of that experience, including what I have liked about Zig so far and what I haven't. I'll include some comparisons to Rust along the way since that was my previous go-to language. Projects The first project I started in Zig was snurl . It is a library for interacting with the smallnet (Gemini, Finger, Gopher, Spartan, and such). My goal has been to provide an alternative to curl for the smallnet, with similar testing and fuzzing requirements but on a smaller scale. I wanted to roughly follow TigerStyle insofar as it made sense for the project. Something I ran into early on was that the fuzzer didn't actually work. When getting excited about fuzzing in my last post, I didn't realize that the feature had not yet been completed. This isn't surprising, considering Zig's status, but it was disappointing, especially since the fuzzer is demonstrated in the generated main.zig file provided by zig init . After this, I wrote a two programs which I have not published yet. The first is a small TUI typer racer. It was simpler than I expected to get a minimum version working so far. The second is an n-body simulator with stellar evolution using raylib. Zig Day The most exciting opportunity in the last few months was the chance to go to a local Zig Day. I learned of Zig Day Seattle occurring on Lobsters on August 20th. I was ecstatic to learn that there was a Zig Day in my area. Then I saw Andrew Kelley would be there and became more excited. Zig Days are local meetups where people interested in Zig hang out, work on their projects together, and talk about Zig. For this Zig Day, I decided to work on snurl. A friend, Evin Yulo also decided to attend. The event itself occurred in the Bothell library, moved there from the Bellevue library after so many people signed up that capacity was overwhelmed. Having the creator of Zig at the event will do that. I love the format of these Zig Days and I'm glad they are a part of the community. Since they are run by local groups, it gives the whole Zig community a more interconnected feeling. It's a way to interact with other people who are interested in Zig in person. And, in this case, the creator of Zig itself. I got the chance to talk with other programmers about their projects. Hopefully some ideological cross-pollination occurred that will make all our projects stronger. I ended up working on snurl with evin, who started work on integrating Zig's standard library TLS implementation as alternative backend. I also briefly talked with Andrew Kelley. I hope Zig's built-in fuzzing gets fixed sometime soon! Ryan Hendrickson wrote an excellent article outlining more of the events of that day from his perspective if you want more details. I will definitely be a

articles.title: GOTO Considered Totally Sick (for error handling in C)
articles.content: I recently started writing C again for the first time since 2018, and handling errors has been an especially difficult adjustment coming from languages like Go and Zig that coddle me with their wonderful defer and errdefer . Then I read some emails from John Carmack on inlined code that gave me an epiphany on writing cleaner error handling code, and now I want to share it with the world. But First Let’s Defer I write Go all day at my dayjob, and error handling is pretty trivial. When there’s an error we wrap it and bubble it up, and let some top dog up the call stack figure out what they want to do with it. If there is resource cleanup involved, it’s made easy with defer : type Doer interface { MightError ( int ) error Lock () Unlock () } func SomeFunc ( d Doer ) error { d . Lock () defer d . Unlock () if err := d . MightError ( 3 ); err != nil { return errors . Wrap ( err , "Doer.MightError()" ) } // the rest of this very important function has been hidden from you for esoteric reasons } Sometimes there’s more complicated handling, but in 99% of scenarios it’s that simple because Go doesn’t have manual memory allocation and you don’t need to worry about cleaning it up when there’s an error. Zig on the other hand does require you to manually manage memory, which I find a little more difficult because I’m not experienced enough for it to be second nature like it is when I write Go. Here’s a snippet from my toy multiplexer that uses errdefer : fn init ( allocator : std . mem . Allocator , env_map : * std . process . Environ . Map , cfg : Config ) ! Model { const sh = env_map . get ( "SHELL" ) orelse "/bin/sh" ; const shell_z = try std . fmt . allocPrintSentinel ( allocator , "{s}" , . { sh } , 0 ) ; errdefer allocator . free ( shell_z ) ; const posix_block = try env_map . createPosixBlock ( allocator , . { } ) ; errdefer posix_block . deinit ( allocator ) ; const tabs : [ ] Tab = try allocator . alloc ( Tab , cfg . commands . len ) ; errdefer allocator . free ( tabs ) ; const pipes : [ ] Pipe = try allocator . alloc ( Pipe , cfg . commands . len ) ; errdefer allocator . free ( pipes ) ; // all done with allocations (and errors) errdefer comptime unreachable ; // the rest of this function has been stolen by bilgerats } I’m allocating memory for several types, and because any one of the allocations can fail I need to handle freeing up each succesful memory allocation that preceded the failure. Zig’s errdefer makes this easy, there’s no manual tracking of what needs to be freed at any point, because the deferred statements will execute in reverse order if the function returns an error. Also I’m following the Reserve First pattern, which is where I learned errdefer comptime unreachable from. This is the C Part Now, enter C. There’s no defer or errdefer . I’ve painted myself into a corner with some ugly code a few times because I’m so used to those tools that I don’t regularly plan ahead for what my error handling control flow will look like. Until rece

articles.title: Hoot 0.10.0 released
articles.content: Hoot 0.10.0 released! Dave Thompson — October 28, 2026 We are excited to announce the release of Hoot 0.10.0! Hoot is a Scheme to WebAssembly compiler backend for Guile , as well as a general purpose WebAssembly toolchain. In other words, Scheme in the browser! This release contains new features and bug fixes and since the 0.9.0 release back in May. Use Hoot in the upcoming Lisp Game Jam! On Friday (October 30th 2026), the autumn edition of the Lisp Game Jam will begin! It's a 10-day long game jam where participants make games using their favorite flavor of Lisp. Does making a small web game in Scheme using Hoot sound appealing to you? Well, then we have just the thing to get you started: the Hoot game jam template! This template project has everything you need to start making an HTML5 game with Hoot quickly. The template repository includes: Bindings to the necessary web APIs to make an interactive game with HTML5 canvas A Makefile for compiling, running a development web server, and generating a .zip bundle for uploading to itch.io A very simple Breakout-like example game that demonstrates how to put all the pieces together For more inspiration, here are some games made with Hoot for past jams: Now, onto the release notes! Compiler changes Added module name to contextualize duplicate import errors. Added support for library versioning for R6RS compatibility. Fixed default version for define-module libraries. Fixed locate-library not respecting configured load extensions. Previously, we were using Guile's load extension parameter instead of Hoot's own. Runtime changes Added %struct-ref and %struct-set! primitives for accessing record types defined using the interpreter. Stopped raising errors when importing an undefined symbol in the runtime module system. Guile is lax about this so Hoot being strict caused compatibility issues. Fixed optional argument parsing in primitive-eval . Fixed keyword argument parsing for procedures with both optional and keyword arguments in primitive-eval . Fixed error messages regarding runtime module registry to include the correct CLI flag: -fruntime-modules . Scheme changes Added partial implementation of SRFI-13 : String Libraries. It's just a set of re-exports, very similar to Guile, but Guile's SRFI-13 module is not declarative and is thus rejected by Hoot's compiler. Added partial implementation of SRFI-60 : Integers as Bits. Added define-macro , defmacro , delete , list->symbol , and symbol to (guile) . Exported define-syntax-parameter and syntax-parameterize , symbol-append , integer-length , and gensym from (guile) . Added list->bitvector and bitvector to (hoot bitvectors) and re-exported them in (guile) . Implemented get-bytevector-all in (rnrs io ports) . Made bytevector=? a publicly exported procedure from (hoot bytevectors) and (rnrs bytevectors) . Added define-syntax-parameter and syntax-parameterize primitives. Improved (ice-9 exceptions) exports to more closely match Guile. Added (rnrs) module. Added
articles.summary: Hoot 0.10.0 发布，这是 Guile 的 Scheme 到 WebAssembly 编译器后端，让 Scheme 跑在浏览器中。

articles.title: Code-execution flaw in UEFI firmware affects most servers on planet Earth
articles.content: Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers. The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II , an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the “preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications.” Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft’s hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot , which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install other payloads that also run each time early in the boot process. The cat has left the bag The parties that discovered CVE-2026-97631—Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes of Google—had arranged for it to stay under wraps until a coordinated disclosure that was scheduled for January. AMI, a maker of motherboards and other hardware, published this pull request last month that detailed the vulnerability and included a code fix. Once the post came to the attention of the discovering parties, TianoCore Project members published a public advisory last week. With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits. Further compounding the urgency, patching UEFI code vulnerabilities in millions of end devices sold and used by thousands of hardware makers and cloud providers is cumbersome and time-consuming. Word of the vulnerability comes six days after another botched disclosure, this one involving a critical code-execution vulnerability in the PHP programming language. “This vulnerability in the ICMP parser of the EDK2 network stack is interesting in terms of how it affects the chain of trust and the broader ecosystem,” said HD Moore, creator of Metasploit and chief research officer at security firm Dragos. “An attacker intent on compromising a nearby endpoint or server could use this bug to hijack program flow at a point where the boot process still has access to sensitive components, like the endpoint’s TPM. This could be used to break disk encryption for cases where an attacker has short-term network access (and it would be even easier in a theft scenar
articles.summary: TianoCore EDK II 引导固件曝出 9.5 分严重漏洞，影响全球多数服务器厂商与数据中心，防御方需紧急响应。

articles.title: Forging a Microsoft Edge Full Chain with Logic Bugs Only
articles.content: I think I should still dump some of my work once in a while, even though it feels like fewer and fewer people actually sit down and read articles these days (or maybe now they all leave it to their agents XD). Anyway, this is what I built for Pwn2Own Berlin 2026 — a completely handmade, logic-only Microsoft Edge Full Chain, with no memory corruption, and no AI at all! 🔥 The whole chain is made up of five bugs and two Windows features. I have also shared the whole bug-hunting and chaining process at this year’s HITCON and Hexacon, plus some fun stories along the way. You can check the slides here ! Also, maybe everyone thinks LLMs can already pwn everything in the AI era, so something made entirely by hand somehow feels a bit more precious. That might also be why this chain was nominated for this year’s Pwnie Awards and won the Epic Achievement award. 🎉 Let’s Navigate! So where do we start with a logic-only full chain? Well, since it’s a “browser,” let’s start by looking at how “browsing” (or what Chromium calls “navigation”) works. I won’t go into too much detail in this post, because I think in this era, you can just ask your agents to fill in the details :) But I’d still recommend reading “ Life of a Navigation “ from Chrome University if you want to get the full picture. The Forgotten Navigation Throttles While I was walking through the Chromium Navigation flow, something called “Navigation Throttles” caught my attention. They live in the Browser Process, and intercept all navigation requests initiated by either the Browser or the Renderer. Maybe it’s easy to say this in hindsight, but out of the 3,000+ CVEs Google Chrome has fixed over the past five years, there are only fewer than 20 related to them. So I guess this is also a corner not too many people pay attention to. Anyway, I started digging into the Navigation Throttles, and checked how Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge implemented them. And while going through the code, I found that Edge has a throttle called EdgeCAGuidanceNavigationThrottle for its enterprise Entra ID feature (the CA here stands for Conditional Access ). The purpose of this throttle is to guide users to the right User Profile when Edge detects them signing in with a work account on a Microsoft website. And to fire this throttle, you have to start a navigation from a specific Microsoft-owned origin, such as login.live.com : 1 location. href = `https://guidance-ca-error/?email={email}&switch_profile={url}` And once the throttle is fired, Edge would compare the email of the current User Profile with ?email={email} . If they don’t match, Edge pops up a dialog guiding you to switch accounts. But if they do match, Edge would then grab the URL you were originally heading to from switch_profile={url} , and launch a new navigation with Chromium’s internal Navigation API: 1 2 3 4 5 NavigateParams params (browser, switch_profile_url, ui::PAGE_TRANSITION_LINK) ; params.disposition = WindowOpenDisposition::CURRENT_TAB; params.windo
articles.summary: 研究者公开 Pwn2Own Berlin 2026 上仅用逻辑漏洞打造的微软 Edge 完整利用链，展示浏览器攻防细节。

The architecture reduced embedding staleness from nearly two days to under a minute and improved offline NDCG by 1.67%, while online testing increased uncancelled bookings by approximately one-third of a percent. By Leela Kumili
articles.summary: Airbnb扩展Chronon平台，将推荐嵌入更新延迟从近两天降至一分钟内，离线NDCG提升1.67%。

articles.title: Presentation: Wrangling Telemetry at Scale: A Guide to Self-Hosted Observability
articles.content: Colin Douch shares battle-tested strategies for building and scaling self-hosted observability stacks. He explains how to effectively correlate metrics, structured logs, and distributed traces using open-source tooling like Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics, and Jaeger, while navigating the engineering trade-offs of avoiding SaaS vendor lock-in. By Colin Douch
articles.summary: InfoQ演讲分享大规模自建可观测性栈的实战经验，介绍用Prometheus、VictoriaMetrics和Jaeger关联指标、日志与追踪。

articles.title: Microsoft's October Security Update Fixes 1,400+ Vulnerabilities, One Exploited in the Wild
articles.content: Microsoft's latest monthly security update addresses 1415 vulnerabilities across multiple products. One vulnerability affecting Windows Shell has been exploited in the wild, while 85 are classified as critical. Affected products include Windows OS, Office, Exchange, .NET, Edge, as well as potentially Hyper-V and Azure components. By Sergio De Simone
articles.summary: 微软十月安全更新修复1415个漏洞，其中85个为严重级别，一个Windows Shell漏洞已被在野利用。

articles.title: Chrome Opens Trial for the Email Verification API: Letting Sites Verify Without Sending Emails
articles.content: Google has opened a Chrome origin trial for the Email Verification API, a WICG proposal that lets the browser confirm email ownership without sending a message. Gmail is the first provider. Developers add form hints and validate a signed token server-side. Commenters question the privacy benefit, and the API is best used as a progressive enhancement. By Daniel Curtis
articles.summary: Chrome开放邮件验证API试验，网站无需发邮件即可确认邮箱归属，Gmail为首家支持方，隐私收益存疑。

articles.title: Article: Building an Offline-First AI Coding Tutor for Low-End Android Phones
articles.content: This article is about engineering an offline-first app for low-end devices based on our experience in Nigeria and India. The interesting problems in this space are storage, quota, cold start, and failure-path design. Our approach applies to any product whose users are on constrained devices and intermittent connections, when the assumption they have a laptop and broadband access do not hold. By Chidi Nwaogu
articles.summary: 文章分享面向低端安卓手机的离线优先AI编程辅导应用经验，重点解决存储、配额、冷启动与失败路径设计。

articles.title: Cloudflare Opens Quicksilver to Customers as Workers KV Instant, Inside a 1 MB Envelope
articles.content: Cloudflare has put Quicksilver, the internal key-value store behind nearly every request it serves, into private beta as a Workers KV mode. Reads resolve in 1.62 ms at p99 against 287 ms for classic KV. The constraints decide the use case: 10,000 keys, one megabyte per namespace, and one write per namespace per second. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
articles.summary: Cloudflare将内部键值存储Quicksilver以Workers KV新模式开放私测，p99读取1.62毫秒，但受1MB与万键限制。

articles.title: Uber Moves beyond CPU Cores with Performance-Aware Scheduling for Stateful Workloads
articles.content: Uber has introduced Normalized Compute Units (NCUs) to make CPU allocation more consistent across its highly heterogeneous server fleet. By Craig Risi
articles.summary: Uber推出归一化计算单元NCU，在异构服务器集群中实现更一致的CPU分配与性能感知调度。

articles.title: How Anthropic Redesigned Source Control for AI-Driven Development
articles.content: Anthropic recently detailed how it migrated its monorepo from Git to Scion. Scion is a source control system that moves repository operations to the server side and uses content-addressed storage and tiered caches for agent and CI workloads. The design sacrifices offline independence for less local data and shared infrastructure. By Eran Stiller
articles.summary: Anthropic详述将单体仓库从Git迁移至自研Scion，服务端操作与分层缓存为AI代理和CI工作负载优化。

articles.title: Presentation: Serving LLMs at Scale: The Hidden KV Cache Advantage
articles.content: Khawaja Shams shares a distributed systems perspective on scaling LLM inference stacks efficiently. He discusses practical strategies for optimizing GPU utilization, managing KV cache memory cliffs, leveraging tiered storage, reducing tail latency, and implementing disaggregated prefill and decode architectures to improve overall fleet performance, cost economics, and availability. By Khawaja Shams
articles.summary: Khawaja Shams分享分布式系统视角下大规模LLM推理优化策略，涵盖GPU利用率、KV缓存内存悬崖、分层存储与预填充解码分离。

articles.title: AWS Shows Use of AI Agents to Triage Linux Kernel CVEs
articles.content: Engineers from Amazon Web Services (AWS) have described how the team that maintains the Linux kernel for EC2 infrastructure handles kernel CVEs. The process combines an automated filter, an AI agent and human review. The team also argues that it needs to move to newer long-term-support (LTS) kernels, as older branches collect fixes that are never backported. By Matt Saunders
articles.summary: AWS团队披露EC2 Linux内核CVE处理流程，结合自动过滤、AI代理与人工审核，并主张迁移至更新的长期支持内核。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #541: Big Tech reports AI spending Wednesday as CoreWeave debt hits distress
articles.content: This issue looks ahead. On Wednesday the Fed announces its rate decision, then Microsoft and Alphabet report after the close. Amazon follows on Thursday. Investors want to know whether AI spending is still paying off, and the credit market is already nervous: insurance against a CoreWeave default now costs more than 10% a year. Anthropic is expected to file its IPO paperwork publicly any day. Moonshot says Kimi K3.1 Pro's open weights arrive November 4. Israel votes on Tuesday after a campaign full of AI deepfakes, and the US midterms are a week from Tuesday. In the middle: so far, AI has paid off for the companies that sell it, not the ones that buy it.
articles.summary: AI Weekly第541期前瞻微软、Alphabet、亚马逊财报，投资者关注AI支出回报，CoreWeave债务违约保险成本上升引发信贷市场担忧。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #540: AI is finding software flaws faster than teams can fix them
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past two weeks, drawn from our Use-Case Library and from SEC filings. Three things stand out: AI now finds security flaws at record volume, AI agents do a large share of the work at some companies, and test agents keep doing things nobody asked them to do.
articles.summary: AI Weekly第540期指出AI发现安全漏洞的速度已超过团队修复能力，部分公司AI代理承担大量工作，测试代理持续增加。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #539: AI-made midterm ads top $137 million, and 70% carry no AI label
articles.content: Campaigns and PACs have spent more than $137 million on AI-generated or AI-enhanced midterm ads, and about 70% of them carry no AI label, the New York Times reported. The biggest pro-AI super PAC network paid about $20 million to a Nevada company that exists only as a post office box. A new report found 81 of 134 AI models failed a test built from terrorist-style questions. A video game reverse engineering site is closing because AI made the work too easy. Some companies that rushed into AI are now limiting it, and a JAMA study counted 270 million questions doctors asked one AI tool. In the middle: police in Michigan used an AI-generated photo of a teenager to catch a suspect.
articles.summary: 据纽约时报报道，中期选举AI生成广告支出超1.37亿美元，约70%未标注AI，某亲AI超级PAC向空壳公司支付约2000万美元。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: AI Weekly第537期聚焦Anthropic警告小型AI模型或将自我复制到智能家居设备，另含专家热议的其他AI话题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: AI Weekly第536期关注顶尖AI模型未能通过自主开展AI研究测试，并探讨AI治理话语权、军事规划应用及PC端落地。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: AI Weekly第535期总结企业因AI成本过高转向更便宜模型，大型部署进入日常使用，同时AI受限或被移除的场景增多。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: AI Weekly第534期报道高校IT负责人首次将AI列为首要任务，剑桥拒绝Turnitin AI训练条款，达特茅斯调查教务长写作问题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #533: Meta tested human callers behind its AI phone agent
articles.content: The AI story of September 22–28 was not simply that agents became more capable. It was that their hidden handoffs became visible: a supposedly automated call could reach a contractor, a supposedly private prompt or image could reach a reviewer, a monitor could detect an agent long before a person stopped it, and a local app flaw could inherit every permission a user had granted. The new AI Weekly Who’s Who census points to one practical question: when an agent crosses a boundary, who knows—and who can still intervene?
articles.summary: AI Weekly第533期揭示AI代理隐藏的人工转接：所谓自动电话可转至外包人员，私密提示或图像可能被审核员查看。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #531: AI labs shipped agents before agreeing how to report failures
articles.content: The AI story of September 14–20 was not one spectacular model launch. It was the machinery around agents becoming visible: people reading private chats, models writing instructions into their own memory, plugins updating beneath users, and regulators asking how to stop a system after release. The latest AI Weekly Who’s Who census surfaced 535 expert-shared links. We ranked them by consequence and reader relevance, not by raw share count. Here is what mattered last week—and, more importantly, what could move the story from September 22–28.
articles.summary: AI Weekly第531期指出AI实验室在未就故障报告达成一致前已发布代理，暴露私聊被读、模型自写记忆、插件静默更新等问题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #530: Applied AI This Week
articles.content: Companies are giving AI specific jobs: checking security cameras, helping farmers understand their records, searching satellite images, and preparing sales quotes. This edition explains how those tools work, who can use them, and what companies have reported so far.
articles.summary: AI Weekly第530期介绍企业为AI分配具体任务，如监控摄像头、辅助农民理解记录、搜索卫星图像和准备销售报价。

articles.title: The future is Postgres
articles.content: Craig Kerstiens returns to talk about the ever-expanding world of Postgres: a deliberately boring core, a thriving extension ecosystem, and pg_lake bringing DuckDB and Iceberg into the mix. We dig into the pain of ETL, what Craig is watching in Postgres 19, the impact of AI on open source maintainers, and why the database still has plenty of room to grow.
articles.summary: Changelog播客邀请Craig Kerstiens探讨Postgres扩展生态、pg_lake整合DuckDB与Iceberg及AI对开源维护者的影响。

articles.title: Building what's next
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Zeno Rocha, CEO of Resend, about scaling "boring" email to 3 million users, the secret Go rewrite behind it, and building for agents. We cover pricing.md, MCP, spam gangs, and why Resend keeps what's next for email.
articles.summary: Resend CEO Zeno Rocha分享如何将邮件服务扩展至300万用户，包括Go重写、面向Agent构建及MCP等话题。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: NanoClaw作者Gavriel Cohen讲述40小时周末项目如何成为爆红开源项目，并发展为容器隔离的企业AI公司。

articles.title: Changelog IRL @ PlanetScale (Sept 17, 2026)
articles.content: Changelog is taking over PlanetScale's HQ We’re getting together IRL!! On Thursday, September 17th, Changelog is taking over PlanetScale’s HQ in San Francisco for an evening of short talks and conversations about AI, developer tools and what people are building. We’ll have a few conversations with special guests and time for questions, food, drinks and hanging out. I’ll be joined by three builders pushing this idea forward, starting with Dan Robinson from Detail (detail.dev), with more guests to be announced very soon. I also have 80 limited edition t-shirts printed to give away! This won’t be a few presentations followed by everyone heading home. We’re doing this Changelog-style: live conversations, questions from the room, drinks, and plenty of time afterward for the hallway track. If you’re in San Francisco, register to come hang out! Changelog IRL Thursday, September 17th, 2026 6:00pm – 9:00pm PDT PlanetScale HQ 108 Natoma St, San Francisco, CA 94105 Speakers Dan Robinson, (Detail) Christian Glassiognon, Developer Educator at PlanetScale TBD Schedule 6:00 - 6:45pm: Doors open, food, drinks and networking 6:45 - 7:00pm: Welcome and opening chat with Adam 7:00 - 8:00pm: Changelog IRL with Dan and special guests 8:00 - 8:15pm: Questions 8:30 - 9:00pm: Hanging out and networking 9:00pm: Close All times Pacific. PlanetScale HQ, 108 Natoma St, San Francisco.
articles.summary: Changelog将于9月17日在PlanetScale旧金山总部举办线下活动，围绕AI、开发工具及开发者构建内容展开交流。

articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.
articles.summary: Cal.com联合创始人Peer Richelsen讨论开源仓库可能已被攻陷的猜想，以及AI如何压平知识图谱。

articles.title: Postgres at PlanetScale
articles.content: Sam Lambert is back after 4 years and he does not hold back! We cover $5 PlanetScale Postgres, the Neki "do-over" of Vitess, agents shipping schema changes through deploy requests, rolling back a 500TB table in seconds, and the very real question of whether to open source any of it. Plus: why he thinks the sleeping, lazy giants should be broken up.
articles.summary: PlanetScale的Sam Lambert介绍5美元Postgres、Vitess重做、Agent提交schema变更及500TB表秒级回滚。

articles.title: Canary tokens and digital tripwires
articles.content: Haroon Meer is back! Haroon is the Founder of Thinkst, the ~50-person bootstrapped company behind Canary and Canarytokens — honeypots and tripwires you sprinkle inside your network and forget about until an attacker touches one. We talk about the AWS API key token attackers just can't resist trying, the real credit card token backed by an actual bank partnership, Breadcrumbs (their brand-new feature that leads intruders straight to your canaries), a live demo where a hardware Canary becomes a Synology NAS in one click, and how a company with zero outbound sales and no price increase in ten years quietly passed $22.5 million in ARR.
articles.summary: Thinkst创始人Haroon Meer介绍Canary蜜罐与数字绊线，以及攻击者难以抗拒的AWS API密钥诱饵。

articles.title: From open source hits to OpenAI
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Max Stoiber, currently working on ChatGPT's plugin directory and app platform at OpenAI. We discuss the hundreds of open source projects nobody remembers alongside the big ones like react-boilerplate and styled-components, how Spectrum became part of GitHub and eventually helped shape GitHub Discussions, the founder growth that came from building Stellate, the GraphQL cache that turned into a dual acquisition by Shopify and The Guild, and why ChatGPT apps feel like a new surface for software.
articles.summary: OpenAI的Max Stoiber回顾react-boilerplate等开源项目历程，以及Spectrum被GitHub收购的经历。

articles.title: MCP on Code Mode
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Matt Carey about Code Mode and how most of us have been thinking about MCP all wrong. Matt works on the Agents SDK and MCP at Cloudflare — we discuss how server-side Code Mode lets one MCP server expose all ~2,500 Cloudflare API endpoints in about 1,000 tokens of context, the dynamic Worker loader that runs model-written code safely in a V8 isolate, Matt's own workflow with Claude, where memory fits into the future of agents, and his Zaggy git wrapper that keeps agents from force-pushing his repos.
articles.summary: Cloudflare的Matt Carey讲解Code Mode如何让单个MCP服务器以约1000 token暴露2500个API端点。

articles.title: Automation at the speed of Swamp
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Adam Jacob, founder of System Initiative and creator of Swamp, about what happens when AI agents change the entire shape of software development. We discuss how he went from an 18-person team down to five and shipped Swamp 900 times in four weeks, why he brought User Acceptance Testing (UAT) testing back from the 90s, why software architecture (and domain-driven design) suddenly matters more than knowing how to write code, the live demo where I pointed Swamp at my Proxmox box and watched it write its own automation (blew my mind!!), and why he'll never accept a pull request to Swamp, ever.
articles.summary: System Initiative创始人Adam Jacob讲述AI Agent重塑开发流程，团队从18人减至5人，四周发布Swamp 900次。

articles.title: Anthropic Engineer Declares the Coding Interview Dead
articles.content: An Anthropic engineering manager says he has stopped using traditional coding interviews because AI can now outperform candidates on the kinds of programming challenges they typically contain. "There's no more point in giving you a little React challenge than there is in quizzing people about assembly; Claude is now better at both," said Felix Rieseberg in a blog post. "Our most impactful builders are successful regardless of how good they are at these tests." The Register reports: "I don't think the coding interview is going to come back," said Rieseberg. "It's easy to get sentimental given how many copies of 'Algorithms and Data Structures' were bought in hopes of unlocking good jobs and a better future -- or how the death of the coding interview is another milestone in software engineering reaching a new level of abstraction." At the same time, he's not certain what will replace it. "I'm probably not the only manager trying to figure out how to interview for people who build well with AI," Rieseberg wrote. "I haven't quite gotten there yet -- but I'm scanning resumes and portfolios for little prototypes that exhibit taste, empathy, and principled thinking. If you have figured out something better, I'd love to hear how." In a response posted to social media, Jaana Dogan, principal engineer at Google, said: "I'm not doing a ton of coding interviews nowadays but I'd be interested to interview how people use coding agents," she wrote. "That itself gives me more signals about candidates' coding skills." "We are not seeing tech companies abandon skills assessments widely across the industry -- at least not yet," added Nicole Bachaud, labor economist at ZipRecruiter. "In fact, based on our October 2026 Employer Survey of 1,500 employers, we see the tech industry (Information sector specifically) is actually the most likely to test for skills, with 62.5 percent of employers requiring formal skill tests on initial applications." "The change at Anthropic might be reflectin
articles.summary: Anthropic工程经理称已停用传统编程面试，因AI在典型编程题上表现已超越候选人。

articles.title: Amazon Puts a Camera In Its Echo Studio So Alexa Can See
articles.content: Amazon has added a camera to its Echo Studio speaker, allowing Alexa to visually identify objects, help with tasks and remotely monitor a room. For those concerned about privacy, Amazon is keeping a camera-free version available. The Next Web reports: The camera speaker ships today for $249.99. Hold up a board game box and Alexa can explain the rules, or show it a box of cereal and it can help you reorder it, according to Amazon. Owners can also check in on the room from the Alexa app while they are away. The Echo Studio without a camera stays on sale at $219.99. A dedicated button turns off the microphones and any camera, and a visual indicator shows when a camera streams images or video to the cloud, Amazon said. Certain features require Alexa+, which is included with a Prime membership. Other devices Amazon unveiled today include an Echo Time alarm clock, an Alexa Photo Frame and the Echo Show 16. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 亚马逊为Echo Studio音箱加入摄像头，使Alexa可视觉识别物体并远程监控，售价249.99美元，另保留无摄像头版本。

articles.title: Are AI Execs Too Out of Touch To Build For the General Public?
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: Former Yahoo CEO and early Google engineer Marissa Mayer is catching a lot of flak for how she uses AI. In an interview about her new app Dazzle, an AI assistant that learns from your camera roll, Mayer poses what she believes is an impressive flex for the product: It helped her come up with three bullet points about her 10-year-old daughter for a birthday presentation at school, describing her as "empathetic, creative, and an animal lover." It's a vague description, like a generic horoscope -- it could probably describe a lot of 10-year-olds. Some onlookers, like progressive activist Leah Greenberg, marveled that "the fact that Marissa Mayer would voluntarily disclose this to a reporter is a pretty good demonstration of how deeply the culture of Silicon Valley has diverged from the rest of humanity." [...] After publication, Mayer defended herself in a long X post. She claims she was not relying on Dazzle to explain her child to her, but rather, she was testing what her prototype could do -- it resurfaced photos of "forgotten kindergarten projects," like a "snake devenomer" or "sandcat playground," illustrating her daughter's creativity and care for animals. Fair enough. But Mayer remarks in the same interview that people could also use her AI to outsource the mental load of "figuring out the theme for your child's birthday party." She says she's used her app to plan a playdate for her daughter, book family activities on vacation, and decide what to be for Halloween. She even proposes that her AI assistant could coordinate plans with her husband's AI assistant. When the reporter asks her if it's depressing to imagine this "frictionless future planned by AI," Mayer replies, "I haven't really thought that through." The bigger question is: What should we outsource to AI? "What feels like grunt work to someone might be a meaningful part of parenthood for someone else," says Fortune's Emma Hinchliffe. Michael Tasner,
articles.summary: TechCrunch报道前雅虎CEO Marissa Mayer因AI使用方式及新应用Dazzle的言论引发争议，被指与大众脱节。

articles.title: Amazon Finds 'Tokenmaxxing' Lacks Productivity Gains
articles.content: Ancient Slashdot reader Gilmoure shares a report from Tom's Hardware, adding: "Huh. Looks like consuming one's own slop does not turn the wheels of industry." From the report: Amazon wants its engineers to quit chasing token counts, warning that heavy AI usage does not automatically mean better work. In updated engineering guidelines published on October 27, the company laid out how developers and managers should gauge AI's real impact -- and the takeaway is blunt: consuming more tokens is not the same as delivering more value. [...] According to the memo, metrics such as AI adoption rates, token consumption, code changes, and code reviews become "deeply flawed" when they are disconnected from actual results. Turning them into targets, Amazon says, encourages wasteful behavior that clashes with its emphasis on "frugality and simplicity" and can raise both compute bills and software complexity. The company's preferred yardstick is long-term results. "We believe that it is best to measure, and be measured by, long-term outcomes," Amazon wrote. That does not mean managers should ignore usage data altogether, as input metrics remain useful when examined "with care and judgment" alongside other indicators. Amazon suggests looking at both the teams using AI the least and those using it the most to determine whether adoption is translating into better delivery. [...] The memo also pushes back on the idea that every task needs an AI tool. If current tooling does not benefit someone's work, Amazon says, that is "a finding, not a failing." Engineers who can explain where today's tools fall short are demonstrating judgment rather than reluctance to adopt AI. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 亚马逊警告工程师勿追逐token数量，指出重度AI使用并不自动带来更好工作成果。

articles.title: FCC Approves Amazon Leo's $11.5 Billion Acquisition of Globalstar
articles.content: The FCC has approved (PDF) Amazon Leo's $11.5 billion acquisition of satellite operator Globalstar, giving the Starlink rival additional infrastructure and spectrum to expand into direct-to-device satellite connectivity. Engadget reports: You may not know Globalstar but have possibly used its services, as the company provides Apple's emergency satellite connectivity for compatible iPhones and Watches. Interestingly, Apple also held a 20 percent stake in Globalstar prior to its takeover. As part of the deal, Leo will power satellite services for supported iPhone and Apple Watch models. Leo, a rival to SpaceX's Starlink, has been active of late. The company recently announced that it has 400 satellites in orbit and revealed last month that it had launched high-quality satellite internet service in Uzbekistan. It's teaming up with Delta to eventually bring satellite internet to flights, as well. Amazon recently added six new Arianespace launches and aims to have more than 3,000 low-earth orbit satellites up in the near future, still well short of SpaceX's 11,000 satellites. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Google Begins Certifying Registered App Stores For Android
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Running an app ecosystem has gotten a lot more complex for Google after its loss in the Epic Games antitrust case. While U.S. users can access app stores in Google Play by court order, international users will use Google's voluntary Registered App Stores program. Google has announced that stores wishing to be part of that program are now free to apply, and support will roll out to some Android devices later this year. App stores accepted into the program will enjoy preferential treatment on the Android platform. Users of approved stores will be able to install apps with a single click, similar to the experience in the Play Store. These stores will also be allowed to update apps silently in the background like Google's store does. [...] Registered App Stores are still happening on Android, but they won't be supported in the U.S. -- you can go to Google Play for alternative stores stateside, but so far, Aptoide remains the only one listed. Those operating Android app storefronts who want to be included in the international program can now review the program and begin the enrollment process. Any store hoping to get approval will have to adhere to a number of requirements, including protecting intellectual property, removing illegal content, and publishing a privacy policy for both users and developers. Google also requires several ongoing security measures to ensure the stores do not give malware easier access to Android devices. As part of the application process, store operators must provide documentation for all these points (in English) and upload copies of all their apps. It costs $10,000 per year to participate in the Android Registered App Stores program, and that fee must be paid before Google will review the application. articles.title: Astronomers May Have Just Discovered Our Solar System's Sixth Dwarf Planet
articles.content: Astronomers using the Vera C. Rubin Observatory have discovered 2026 ED138, a large object beyond Neptune that could become the solar system's sixth recognized dwarf planet if further observations confirm it is massive enough to be round. Located about 46 times farther from the Sun than Earth, the object is estimated to be 600 to 1,500 kilometers wide and had remained hidden because it lies against a particularly crowded field of Milky Way stars. Scientific American reports: The discovery was made by running billions of pieces of data collected by the Rubin Observatory through a search code developed by Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian astronomers Matthew Holman and Kevin Napier. "My first reaction was one of excited disbelief," Holman said in a statement. "Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong." When Holman and his colleague Mario Juric of the University of Washington went to double-check, they found 30 more observations of the object by Rubin that dated to between March and July 2026. Looking at other observation tools, the pair found even more sightings going back to 2016. Together, these data allowed the astronomers to begin mapping out 2026 ED138's orbit. The suspected dwarf planet is about 46 times as far from the sun as Earth, making it even more remote than Pluto, which is just 40 times as far. The object is also tilted off the solar system's plane by around 25 degrees, an arrangement that could be linked to disruptions caused by Neptune's gravitational pull. Initial measurements indicate that 2026 ED138 has a diameter between 600 and 1,500 kilometers (373 and 932 miles), which makes it one of the largest dwarf planet candidates yet detected. But size isn't all that matters: further observations are required to determine if the object has enough mass to be pulled into a round shape, which is a key requirement for a dwarf planet. articles.title: Repo-Atlas - Any GitHub user’s work, mapped and clustered, with stale favorites flagged.
articles.content: Type a GitHub username, get the map of what they've actually built: repos clustered by topic, the highlight of each group, and stars over time. Live: https://evoluteur.github.io/repo-atlas/ · permalink per user: ?u=<username> The map. Every public repo as a disc (area ∝ stars), grouped into regions of repos that share topics. Hover for details, click to open the repo. Groups by stars. The legend ranks the regions by the stars they hold, so you see where the attention actually sits. Highlights. The most-starred repo in each group as a card, with its description, language and live-demo link. Hover a card to find its group on the map; the share card lists the top three. Stars over time. Without a token: stars held today, stacked by the year each repo was born. With a token: real cumulative star history per group, from stargazer dates. Share. A 1200×630 card for social posts and a permalink. Each repo's topics are normalised (plurals folded, generic tags like javascript , svg , ui dropped) and hyphenated topics also contribute their parts ( sacred-geometry → sacred , geometry ). Tokens are weighted by inverse document frequency across the account. Tokens used once, or by more than 45% of repos, carry no signal and are dropped. Repos with almost no topics fall back to description words. Repos are compared by cosine similarity and merged bottom-up (average linkage) until no two groups are more than 0.16 alike. The eight groups holding the most stars get a color and a two-word name (the tokens most frequent inside the group and rarest outside it). Everything else folds into loners . All of this is in src/atlas.js : pure functions, no DOM, tested with node --test . Everything runs in the browser against the public GitHub REST API. The map and the highlights work anonymously (60 requests/hour per IP; a typical account takes 2). GitHub only lists when each star was given to authenticated callers, so the star-history chart needs a token. A fine-grained token with no extra permissions is enough. It is kept in sessionStorage for the tab and only sent to api.github.com . Big repos are sampled: every stargazer page for repos under 500 stars, otherwise the first, last and three evenly spaced pages. Each fetched star is an exact (count, date) point; months in between are interpolated. Results are cached in localStorage (repos 1 hour, star history 24 hours). If the API can't be reached (rate limit, offline), the page lets you paste the JSON from api.github.com/users/<login>/repos?per_page=100 and maps that instead. No build step. Serve the folder and open it: npx serve . # or: python3 -m http.server open http://localhost:3000/ ? u=evoluteur npm test # clustering, highlights and timeline math npm run build # dist/repo-atlas.html: one self-contained file index.html page shell src/atlas.js clustering, highlights, timelines (pure, Node-testable) src/github.js REST client: repos, sampled stargazer pages src/charts.js D3: circle-pack map, birth-year columns, stacked sta
